evidence.title: Development and External Validation of a Machine Learning Model for 10-Year Ischemic Stroke Risk Prediction in Diverse Populations
evidence.outcome: Incremental discrimination gain from adding self-reported race as model input
evidence.effect: Race added small gains only with PRS (BioMe +0.022, P=0.034; AoU +0.006, P=0.052), not without PRS; overlapped with polygenic signal.
evidence.quote: The marginal contribution of self-reported race overlapped with polygenic signal, supporting per-ancestry calibration over universal race-aware model deployment.
evidence.sample_unit: patients (34,987 All of Us development cohort; 10,693 BioMe external validation)

evidence.title: Causal Machine Learning for Personalized Surgical Decision-Making in Aortic Dissection: A National Fairness-Aware Clinical AI Framework
evidence.outcome: Model discrimination with versus without race as an input
evidence.effect: Discrimination preserved with race excluded (AUROC 0.834 vs. 0.836).
evidence.quote: Model discrimination was preserved with race excluded (AUROC 0.834 vs. 0.836).

evidence.title: The Impact of Race, Ethnicity, and Sex on Fairness in Artificial Intelligence for Glaucoma Prediction Models
evidence.outcome: Effect of including versus excluding sensitive attributes on performance and fairness
evidence.effect: Excluding attributes gave better AUROC (0.77-0.82) but worse fairness internally; at external #1 including gave better AUROC but worse fairness; at external #2 including gave both better. Removal did not eliminate bias.
evidence.quote: Since removing sex, race, and ethnicity is not a comprehensive solution to eliminate bias in glaucoma algorithm predictions, it may be reasonable to include them if external validation and thorough subpopulation analyses are performed.

evidence.title: Evaluating machine learning model bias and racial disparities in non-small cell lung cancer using SEER registry data
evidence.outcome: Fairness metrics and model performance with vs without race/ethnicity as predictor
evidence.effect: Excluding race/ethnicity as a predictor in survival and surgery recommendation models improved fairness metrics without degrading model performance; but disparate impact persisted in survival models.
evidence.quote: The exclusion of race/ethnicity as a predictor in the survival and surgery recommendation models improved fairness metrics without degrading model performance.

evidence.title: Awareness of Racial and Ethnic Bias and Potential Solutions to Address Bias With Use of Health Care Algorithms
evidence.outcome: Stakeholder perceptions of race and proxy inputs in clinical algorithms producing biased outputs
evidence.effect: Respondents identified 18 algorithms in use with potential for race- and ethnicity-based bias; themes noted bias arises whether or not race is explicitly included and race is used as a proxy for clinical variables.
evidence.quote: The 7 qualitative themes, with 31 subthemes, included the following: (1) algorithms are in widespread use and have significant repercussions, (2) bias can result from algorithms whether or not they explicitly include race, (3) clinicians and patients are often unaware of the use of algorithms and potential for bias, (4) race is a social construct used as a proxy for clinical variables, (5) there is a lack of standardization in how race and social determinants of health are collected and defined, (6) bias can be introduced at all stages of algorithm development, and (7) algorithms should be discussed as part of shared decision-making between the patient and clinician.
evidence.sample_unit: respondents to request for information (organization representatives and individuals)

evidence.title: Health care professionals' perceptions of machine learning based clinical decision support systems for oesophageal cancer management
evidence.outcome: Relative influence of age and gender in ML model versus clinicians' stated importance
evidence.effect: Age and gender had greater influence on the model than their conscious importance to clinicians would support, although other influential factors agreed between clinicians and the model.
evidence.quote: There was agreement between clinicians and the model in many of the most influential factors in decision making, although age and gender had greater influence on the model than their conscious importance to clinicians would support.

evidence.title: Proxy reliance in large language model decisions is uncalibrated to predictive evidence
evidence.outcome: Whether LLMs rely on proxy features in line with their predictive evidence
evidence.effect: Reliance on proxies is uncalibrated to predictive evidence; social-label suppression is fragile, since in-context examples raise reliance above zero in every model. Accuracy-based evaluation detects none of this.

evidence.title: The Guideline for Building Fair Multimodal Medical AI with Large Vision-Language Model
evidence.outcome: Fairness impact of including demographic and clinical metadata as inputs to multimodal medical AI
evidence.effect: Indiscriminate inclusion of all metadata may negatively impact fairness for protected subgroups. Analysis covered dermatology, radiology and ophthalmology (gender, age, skin tone) and more than 20 clinical attributes in dermatology.
evidence.quote: Our findings reveal that the indiscriminate inclusion of all metadata may negatively impact fairness for protected subgroups and show how multimodal AI utilizes demographic information in metadata to influence fairness.

evidence.title: The Impact of Race, Ethnicity, and Sex on Fairness in Artificial Intelligence for Glaucoma Prediction Models
evidence.effect: Excluding sensitive attributes improved internal AUROC (0.77-0.82) but worsened fairness; removing sex, race, and ethnicity did not eliminate bias.
evidence.quote: We found evidence of bias for sex, race, and ethnicity that was not wholly ameliorated by removing these sensitive attributes as inputs to the models.

evidence.title: Evaluating machine learning model bias and racial disparities in non-small cell lung cancer using SEER registry data
evidence.effect: Including race/ethnicity amplified disparities; excluding it improved fairness metrics without degrading performance.
evidence.quote: The models including race/ethnicity amplified the disparities observed in the data.

evidence.title: Accounting for racial bias and social determinants of health in a model of hypertension control
evidence.venue: BMC medical informatics and decision making
evidence.outcome: Influence of race as a model input on predictions and bias
evidence.effect: Race_Black was the third most important feature (OR 1.94, CI 1.90-1.98); the non-stratified model showed implicit racial disparity.
evidence.quote: We found implicit racial disparity in the non-stratified predictive model.

evidence.title: From Biomedical Datasets to Fairness-Aware Recommendations: An Integrated Data Orchestration Pipeline for Binary Clinical Predictions
evidence.outcome: Whether excluding sensitive attributes removes subgroup effects via proxy variables
evidence.effect: Proxy signals found (age with age group, glucose/BMI); exclusion of sensitive attributes judged insufficient to remove subgroup effects.
evidence.quote: Another important finding is that protected-attribute removal is not a sufficient fairness strategy.

commentary.bottom_line: Four offline studies compared models with and without race or other sensitive inputs and found mixed effects on accuracy and fairness, which suggests the effect of an input has to be measured model by model rather than assumed. No study tested a governance review process that applies an inclusion policy, so evidence for the review step itself is indirect.

perspectives.view: Four offline or simulated studies compared models with and without race or sensitive attributes. Race added a discrimination gain of 0.022 in one cohort only when polygenic scores were present, and exclusion preserved AUROC (0.834 vs. 0.836) in another. Fairness shifted in different directions across sites. Inconsistency and indirectness lower certainty to very low.

In the glaucoma study, removing sex, race, and ethnicity did not eliminate bias. In survival models, disparate impact persisted after race was excluded. A proxy study found subgroup signals carried by age group, glucose, and BMI. These findings suggest that dropping an input may not prevent discriminatory outputs, and they support measuring effects directly.

One benchmark found that language models relied on proxies in ways uncalibrated to predictive evidence, and accuracy-based evaluation detected none of it. Another found that including all metadata may harm subgroup fairness. Reviewers who quantify justified effects would likely need subgroup fairness testing with and without each input across sites, as the glaucoma study did.

Three of the four tests focused on racial and ethnic minority patients, but none reported Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy groups. A hazard study of 164,041 patients, including safety-net and low-income patients, found Race_Black was the third most important feature (OR 1.94). No study has tested review policies in those settings.

The endorsements point in different directions. Texas SB 1188 requires EHR decision tools to include recorded biological sex. The CHAI guide calls for anti-classification, meaning protected characteristics are not explicitly used to make decisions. An explicit inclusion policy that documents the clinical justification for each input may help reconcile these duties. No study examined compliance with either requirement.

commentary.research_gap: No study evaluated a governance review that applies an inclusion policy to protected or proxy inputs and then tracked patient outcomes or disparities after deployment. Prospective evaluations in live clinical settings would show whether the review changes model choices and reduces discriminatory outputs. These evaluations would need prespecified fairness metrics and would need to include patients covered by Medicaid or served by safety-net systems.
commentary.underserved_note: None of the four tests reported Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and three focused on racial and ethnic minority groups. The only safety-net and low-income data come from a hazard study. The effect of this practice in those populations is therefore unknown.
